precepts.text: The cities of the tribe of Judah toward the south.
precepts.point: Carmel was Judah's and Bashan was Manasseh's.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
Before Obadiah, the class read Jeremiah 50:19: “And I will bring Israel again to his habitation, and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan, and his soul shall be satisfied upon mount Ephraim and Gilead.” To know whose land Carmel and Bashan were, go back to the first dividing of the land in Joshua. Write it down: Carmel was Judah's.

Joshua 15 gives the cities of Judah: “And the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward were Kabzeel, and Eder, and Jagur,” “And Kinah, and Dimonah”. Then jump to verse 55: “Maon, Carmel, and Ziph”. Those belonged to Judah. Judah's lot ran to the south, right up against the coast of Edom.

Jeremiah 50 goes on to say what God will do when he brings us back: “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none; and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found: for I will pardon them whom I reserve.” He wipes away our iniquity and brings us again to our own habitation.

Then watch how things get switched around. Obadiah says “they of the south shall possess the mount of Esau.” The mount of Esau is where Edom used to dwell originally, and we are going to take that whole area. “and they of the plain the Philistines”: we are going to take Palestine. We shall possess the fields of Ephraim and the fields of Samaria. The land is ours by inheritance from the first dividing, and when God brings Israel back it will be possessed even further than it was then.

precepts.text: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families.
precepts.point: In the days of Nehemiah, Jews had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab, and their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod and could not speak in the Jews' language. Why is that? Because the mothers do the raising of the children.

note.label: Deuteronomy 23: Who May Enter the Congregation and the Holy Camp

precepts.why:
“This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families.” Judah's cities are then counted out, “toward the coast of Edom southward”, and the list matters here because Ashdod is in it.

Ashdod was one of the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the inheritance. Israel did not drive out all the inhabitants and lost it, and Zechariah says a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod. So the city where the bastard dwells, the bastard shut out of the congregation of the Lord, was a city that was Judah's own.

precepts.text: Ashdod with her towns and her villages was among the cities given to Judah.
precepts.point: In the days of Nehemiah, Jews had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab, and their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod and could not speak in the Jews' language. Why is that? Because the mothers do the raising of the children.

note.label: Deuteronomy 23: Who May Enter the Congregation and the Holy Camp

precepts.why:
Among the inheritance of Judah: “Ashdod with her towns and her villages, Gaza with her towns and her villages, unto the river of Egypt, and the great sea, and the border thereof”. Ashdod with her towns and villages was given to the tribe of Judah.

But Israel did not drive out all the inhabitants and lost it, and Zechariah says a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod. By Nehemiah's day Jews were marrying wives of Ashdod and their children could not speak in the Jews' language: children of forbidden unions with the nations, the bastard shut out of the congregation to the tenth generation, dwelling in a city that was Judah's inheritance.

precepts.text: The Jebusites said David could not come in hither, but David took the stronghold of Zion, the same is the city of David.
precepts.point: The people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, whom Israel was not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day. They were forced to become our bondservants.

note.label: Joshua 15: The Lot of the Tribe of Judah

precepts.why:
The children of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, and they dwelt with Judah at Jerusalem unto this day. Later on David conquered this place. “And the king and his men went to Jerusalem unto the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land: which spake unto David, saying, Except thou take away the blind and the lame, thou shalt not come in hither: thinking, David cannot come in hither.” The Jebusites thought David could not come in, that he was not getting past those walls.

“Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David.” Whosoever got up to the gutter and smote the Jebusites would be chief and captain. “So David dwelt in the fort, and called it the city of David. And David built round about from Millo and inward.” What Judah could not do in Joshua's day, David did.

precepts.text: Upon the people left of those nations did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day.
precepts.point: The people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, whom Israel was not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day. They were forced to become our bondservants.

note.label: Joshua 15: The Lot of the Tribe of Judah

precepts.why:
“And all the people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, which were not of the children of Israel, Their children that were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel also were not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day.”

The Jebusites that Judah could not drive out did not stay free among us. The people left of those nations, whom Israel was not able utterly to destroy, were forced to become our bondservants under Solomon; that is where “unto this day” ends up for them.

precepts.text: The children of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.
precepts.point: The king of Jerusalem was already among the kings of the land which the children of Israel smote and whose land they possessed, so this fight in Judges is Judah taking the city itself.

note.label: Judges 1: Judah Goes Up First, but the Inhabitants Are Not Driven Out

precepts.why: Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, smote it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire; yet Judah was supposed to drive the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, out of the land, and could not: “the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.” This verse in Judges ties back into the history we just finished reading in Joshua. The city was taken and burned, but its inhabitants were not driven out, and the Jebusites went on dwelling with the children of Judah in it.

precepts.text: Judah's border went up by the valley of the son of Hinnom unto the south side of the Jebusite, the same is Jerusalem.
precepts.point: The king of Jerusalem was already among the kings of the land which the children of Israel smote and whose land they possessed, so this fight in Judges is Judah taking the city itself.

note.label: Judges 1: Judah Goes Up First, but the Inhabitants Are Not Driven Out

precepts.why: Why was it the children of Judah that fought against Jerusalem? Because Jerusalem sat right on Judah’s border. The border “went up by the valley of the son of Hinnom unto the south side of the Jebusite; the same is Jerusalem”. The Jebusite is Jerusalem, and it lay on Judah’s line by the valley of the son of Hinnom, so it fell to Judah to take it, and it was with the children of Judah that the Jebusites ended up dwelling.

precepts.text: The same account word for word: Caleb's offer, and Othniel the son of Kenaz taking Kirjath-sepher and receiving Achsah to wife.
precepts.point: This is a review of the history we just read in Joshua; it was not that many days ago in the reading that we covered this, and it repeats again here at the opening of Judges.

note.label: Judges 1: Judah Goes Up First, but the Inhabitants Are Not Driven Out

precepts.why:
This is a review of the history we just read in Joshua, and here it is word for word: “And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjath–sepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife. And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife.”

It was not that many days ago in the reading that we covered Caleb’s offer and Othniel the son of Kenaz taking Kirjath-sepher and receiving Achsah to wife, and it repeats again here at the opening of Judges, along with Achsah asking her father for springs of water with the south land, and Caleb giving her the upper springs and the nether springs.

precepts.text: As for the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out, and the Jebusites dwelt with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.
precepts.point: Jerusalem is called Jebus here because the Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, still dwelt in it; this is before David rose up and took it from them. When Israel came out of the wilderness, the promised land was inhabited primarily by Canaanites, and the children of Judah could not drive the Jebusites out.

note.label: Judges 19: The Levite's Concubine at Gibeah

precepts.why: Jerusalem is called Jebus here because the Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, still dwelt in it: “As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.” When Israel came out of the wilderness the promised land was inhabited primarily by Canaanites, and Judah could not drive these out. So in the days of the judges the Levite passing by Jebus called it “the city of a stranger, that is not of the children of Israel”, and would not turn in there.

precepts.text: Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjathsepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife; the same kind of offer the king made over Goliath.
precepts.point: The soldiers themselves did not understand that they were the armies of the living God; David, a sheep keeper sent on an errand, knew it. Israel is the army of the Most High, and every army requires order; that is why there are captains and officers, and despising that order is despising the army of the living God.

note.label: 1 Samuel 17: Not by Sword and Spear

precepts.why:
The men of Israel said, “the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father’s house free in Israel.” A prize was on Goliath’s head.

Caleb made a like offer: “He that smiteth Kirjath–sepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.” The same kind of offer the king made over Goliath.

note.label: Joshua 15: The Lot of the Tribe of Judah

points: As for the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out, but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.

Later on David conquered this place. The Jebusites thought David could not come in, that he was not getting past those walls, saying except thou take away the blind and the lame thou shalt not come in hither; nevertheless David took the stronghold of Zion, the same is the city of David, and dwelt in the fort and built round about.

The people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, whom Israel was not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day. They were forced to become our bondservants.
